baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Cannadine questions the causal argument and uneven treatment of power in Queen Victoria
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Cannadine’s 1990 review is the specified critical source. It records disagreement over connections to women’s rights and republicanism, not unanimous judgment or endorsement of the reviewer’s incidental biographical claims.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Connects aristocratic wealth and power to urban development as well as rural landholding.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own interview describes Calthorpe ground rents and Edgbaston, motivating a broader social history of aristocracy.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Treats biography as a balance of private/public life, evidence, proportion and competing historical judgments.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own interview’s ODNB and Thatcher answers explain the method; his acknowledgment of underrepresented women/businesspeople concerns an editorial programme, not sole authorship of dictionary lives.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Burton criticizes Ornamentalism’s novelty claim and its failure to sustain an analysis of metropole–colony interdependence, arguing that it misreads Sinha’s and Catherine Hall’s accounts of empire’s constitutive role in domestic Britain.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Specific criticism in Burton’s own 2002 opening, reproduced as substantive authorial prose under Abstract on a third-party bibliographic page. She acknowledges Cannadine’s citations and declared interconnected model before criticizing its analytical limits. Sinha and Catherine Hall retain their distinct intellectual credit; neither is presented as a coauthor of Burton’s critique. The reproduced opening was freshly read, but the full article, original journal facsimile, Cannadine’s book and the original works of Sinha/Hall were not freshly read. No claim about the article’s unseen conclusion, a personal reply by Cannadine, or a complete rejection of every part of his work.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Armitage describes his and Cannadine’s shared commitment to placing British history in imperial and wider international settings.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2012 account says their views on the field converged while Cannadine was taking his own imperial turn. This is a bounded comparison,not a claim that collegial generosity proves intellectual transmission or that the NACBS report was jointly authored by them. Cannadine’s Ornamentalism remains unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Brewer uses Cannadine’s account of British industrialization as a model for later economic-development policy in his analysis of Cold War modernization.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2010 printed94/n33 cites Cannadine’s The Present and the Past in the English Industrial Revolution,1880–1980, Past and Present103(1984),147–148and152–154, for the discussion including the policy formulation. Brewer separately cites Rostow1971p33 in n35. Cannadine is a scholarly resource for the historical relationship, not credited with endorsing Rostow’s political program; neither original work read.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Queen Victoria frames a sovereign’s life through gender and political power
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Cannadine’s contemporary review establishes this project and also disputes its execution. A qualified biographical contribution based on the review, not full primary-book verification.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Toynbee's Lectures (1884) define the Industrial Revolution as 'the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations', the concept the later debate revises
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Toynbee, Lectures on the Industrial Revolution in England (posthumous, 1884), Saylor transcription without print pages, read by lecture: Lecture I describes 'England on the eve of the Industrial Revolution'; Lecture VIII: 'The essence of the industrial Revolution is the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations which had previously controlled the production and distribution of wealth'; 'The effects of the industrial Revolution prove that free competition may produce wealth without producing well-being.' A reader's warrant: de Vries (1994, p. 249) calls the Industrial Revolution 'By far the most important such monument in economic history'. No claim that Toynbee coined the term or founded the debate; the chain to the 1980s passes through Clapham and Cannadine, unread here.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Named answers: Cannadine, in Joyce's report of the unread review, asked for 'a history of status' and in reply caricatured Joyce's populism (1992–93); Tilly found 'softcore solipsism' and 'a doubt sandwich' (1994); Kirk 'a materialist view' (1994); Eley and Nield, in Joyce's report, equated his questioning of social history 'with contemporary neo-liberalism' (1995); Koditschek a 'class-evacuated analytical approach' (2014)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: The December 1992 review is unread; Joyce's letter (NYRB, 8 April 1993, read) reports that it ended by calling for 'a history of status' rather than 'a history of class' or 'a history of language', and answers that the categories of populism 'are important precisely for their plasticity not despite it' and open 'a history of social unities' that 'will at once be a history of difference'. Cannadine's reply (read) calls the letter 'disappointingly predictable' and caricatures Joyce's position — status 'merely a "rhetorical construction"', class 'rejected because it is a "grand concept"' — as Cannadine's summary of Joyce, not his own view of status or class. Tilly (1994, read in full): 'Joyce tortures himself on a rack of his own manufacture'; 'a doubt sandwich: a hearty slab of old-fashioned research between two layers of uncertainty' (pp. 263–265). Kirk 1994 by title only. Eley and Nield's 'Starting Over' (1995) is unread; the 'neo-liberalism' charge is Joyce's characterisation (1996, p. 96, read), as is their 'denial of creative conversations'; their 2000 essay (read) finds Democratic Subjects 'with no moorings to the densely contextualized studies of working-class life social historians have come to require' (p. 6). Koditschek (JBS 2014, read): 'class-evacuated analytical approach'; still 'Joyce's best, most innovative, and most insightful book—so far'. Mayfield and Thorne's 1993 reply to his note: metadata only. Joyce's own answers are on his entry.
